def: A finite sequence of well-defined instructions that takes an input and produces the correct output for a given problem, in a finite amount of time.
A statement of what the input looks like and what output we want for it. It says nothing about how to get there; one particular input is an instance.
The measure n that running time is expressed in. It depends on the input: the number of array elements, the degree of a polynomial, the bits of a number, or the vertices and edges of a graph.
The number of basic steps an algorithm executes on an input, written as a function T(n) of the input size.
The extra memory an algorithm uses, as a function of the input size.
The leading term of a running time, without its constant factor. It describes how the algorithm behaves for large n; lower-order terms stop mattering as n grows.
The maximum number of steps an algorithm takes on any input of size n.
The minimum number of steps an algorithm takes on any input of size n.
The average number of steps over all inputs of size n, usually assuming each input is equally likely.
A function that, for large n, is at least the actual number of steps (or memory) an algorithm uses. A lower bound works the same way, from below.
The random-access machine: one processor running instructions one after another, where each basic instruction and each memory access costs one step.
Checks the elements one by one from left to right until the target is found or the array ends. Works on any array; O(n).
Searches a sorted array by comparing the target with the middle element and discarding the half that cannot hold it. O(log n).
A bug from a loop bound or index that is one too large or too small, such as while lo < hi instead of lo ≤ hi. Pick one range convention and test the tiny cases.
Splits the range into three with two cuts m1 and m2 and discards one or two thirds per step. Also finds the peak of a unimodal function.
A function that strictly rises and then strictly falls (one maximum), or falls and then rises (one minimum).
Divide a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine their solutions.
A sort that orders elements using only comparisons between pairs of them (is A[i] ≤ A[j]?).
Repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order, so each pass moves the largest remaining element to the end. O(n²).
Takes each element in turn and inserts it into its place in the sorted part to its left. O(n) best case, O(n²) worst case.
Repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next position. O(n²) in every case.
A sort that rearranges the elements inside the array itself, using only O(1) extra memory.
A sort in which elements with equal keys keep their original order.
Splits the array into halves, sorts each recursively, and merges the two sorted halves. O(n log n) in every case; stable, not in-place.
An equation that describes a running time in terms of the running time on smaller inputs, such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn for merge sort.
The element that PARTITION places in its final position, with smaller elements to its left and larger ones to its right.
Partitions the array around a pivot and sorts the two sides recursively. O(n log n) typically, O(n²) in the worst case; in-place, not stable.
A pivot rule: use the median of A[lo], A[mid] and A[hi]. Sorted and reversed inputs then split well.
A binary tree of the comparisons a comparison sort makes, with one leaf for every possible ordering of the input.
Any comparison sort needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons in the worst case, which is Ω(n log n).
The nonempty, contiguous subarray A[i..j] with the largest sum. Divide and conquer finds it in Θ(n log n); one scan that drops negative stretches finds it in Θ(n).
